title: Half-Life
short: In each half-life, half of the remaining nuclei decay; use it to find amounts left and ages.
trouble: Students think a sample is all gone after two half-lives, taking away the same amount each time instead of halving what is left.

blocks.html: Radioactive Decay and Nuclear Equations described what happens to one nucleus. In a sample of billions, the decays follow a steady pattern, the halving kind of change from Exponential Functions.

The half-life is the time it takes for half of the radioactive nuclei in a sample to decay. After each half-life, half of what is left remains: after $n$ half-lives, the fraction left is $\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^{n}$.

A radioactive nucleus does not age. In any given hour, each one has the same small chance of decaying, whether it formed a minute ago or a million years ago. So in each half-life, half of the nuclei that remain decay, whatever their number. The amount drops by the same fraction, not the same amount, in every equal stretch of time, which is exponential decay.

blocks.title: Carbon dating
blocks.q: A piece of old wood has $\tfrac{1}{4}$ as much carbon-14 per gram of carbon as living wood. About how old is it?
steps: A living tree keeps taking in carbon-14; after it dies, its carbon-14 decays without being replaced.

blocks.title: Finding a half-life
blocks.q: A detector counts 800 decays per minute from a sample, and 100 per minute 30 hours later. What is the half-life?

blocks.html: Thinking a sample is all gone after two half-lives, as if each half-life removed the same amount. Each half-life removes half of what is left: after two, a quarter remains; after three, an eighth. Check by halving step by step.
Older books give carbon-14's half-life as 5,730 years; the evaluated value today is about 5,700 years. Watch a sample decay in Build an Atom.
